why: section 13 over doubles the model does not hold (a field): a bitwise operator reads its operands through ToInt32 (ToUint32 for >>>, the low five bits of a shift count) and the ordinary lane's bv32 helpers, so its result is an exact 32-bit integer whatever its operands hold. orflag swaps the operands of | (proved); toint writes ToInt32 as ~~ instead of | 0 (proved); nibble masks then shifts against shifts then masks (proved); twice reads the masked value, an exact integer, as m + m instead of m * 2 (proved: * is exact); uint truncates to an int32 before >>> 0 (proved: ToUint32 of ToInt32 is ToUint32); shift masks its count to five bits, as the operator does (proved); bump writes ++ as += 1 (proved); ratio names the divisor first (proved: the same uninterpreted division on both sides). parity reads & 1 against % 2 on a field: they differ on a negative or a fraction (WITNESS, unproved); orwitness sets another bit (WITNESS). The writes, which the binary64 decision does not encode, stand on the heap lemma alone: setflag writes the field with the operands of | swapped (proved); clearlow clears the low bit by & ~1 against a shift right and left (proved); stamp writes ToInt32 of the field as ~~ against | 0 and ++ as += 1, the two writes in the other order (proved); store writes the masked value doubled, m * 2 against m + m (proved); setwitness sets another bit (WITNESS, unproved).
